extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, and readers interested in retractions and publication ethics (particularly in mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of reasons and signals that lead to retraction of mathematics research papers (plagiarism, duplication, authorship problems, unreliable data, poor citation practices, etc.), illustrated with examples from Retraction Watch posts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of a major part of text and results
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplication of “a major part of text and results” (e.g., publishing the same substantial text/results in proceedings after they had already appeared in a journal) can be grounds for retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an article was retracted from conference proceedings because the author had already published 'a major part of text and results' in a 2010 journal article. Redundant publication of substantial material (whether in conference proceedings or another journal) justifies retraction rather than correction when the overlap is large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism / copy-pasted chunks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of copy/pasted chunks or verbatim material from another author’s paper without appropriate attribution (blatant plagiarism) leads to retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: papers containing copy/pasted chunks from an earlier paper; tipsters (often the original author) may trigger investigations. Plagiarism detection (including specialized software) and confirmation lead journals to retract papers that substantially duplicate others’ work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship misattribution / denial of credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Including another person’s work (e.g., a student’s) without acknowledging them or giving appropriate authorship credit can result in retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a paper was retracted after it was discovered the authors had included a student’s work without acknowledging her. Editors may choose retraction over correction; disputes over whether correction suffices vs retraction are sometimes influenced by editorial considerations (e.g., protecting a journal’s impact factor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundant publication / reuse of previously published material (self-plagiarism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing material from a previous publication without proper citation or disclosure (self-plagiarism / duplication) can cause a paper to be retracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an article was withdrawn because authors reused material from an earlier publication. Both verbatim copying of others’ text and unacknowledged reuse of the authors’ own prior material are treated seriously by journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequate citation / failure to properly reference prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to adequately cite or acknowledge prior related work — even if referenced — can raise questions about the paper’s originality and may lead to correction or retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an author who referenced a source multiple times still had a paper retracted for inadequate citation, prompting debate about when retraction is appropriate versus issuing a correction. Proper, thorough citation and clear attribution are expected to avoid such outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delayed detection of problems / slow editorial response
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant problems (e.g., plagiarism) discovered many years after publication — and handled slowly by editorial offices — can still lead to retraction, but delay is a frequent problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a nine-year-old plagiarism allegation eventually led to retraction after editors used plagiarism-detection software. The posts urge readers to notify editorial offices promptly so suspected problems can be handled more quickly; timeliness of detection and response is an implicit standard for maintaining literature integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unspecified ethical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices that cite vague or unspecified 'ethical problems' are sometimes used as grounds for retraction when details are not publicly disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a paper was retracted because it 'contains some ethical problems.' Such notices can be uninformative; lack of detail in retraction notices is itself noted as an issue in the reporting of retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misused data / unreliable findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of incorrect, misused, or unreliable data or analysis that undermines the paper’s findings can result in retraction for unreliable findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category labels in the posts include 'misused data' and 'unreliable findings.' When the core results are undermined by data or analytic errors, retraction is an appropriate remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor scholarly practice: inadequate literature search
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on inadequate search methods (e.g., using Google alone) instead of proper literature-search procedures can lead to failure to find prior work and subsequent problems (plagiarism/duplication accusations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example post: 'No, math prof, Google isn’t a proper literature search' — emphasizes that proper literature review methods are expected to avoid overlooking relevant prior publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unhelpful / non-transparent retraction notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices that lack clear explanation of the reasons (unhelpful notices) are criticized; transparency in the notice is considered important for the research record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and commentary in the posts note editors’ apologies for late action and call for clearer, more informative notices. Readers are encouraged to contact editorial offices when they identify problems so that notices and corrections can be handled appropriately and transparently.
